{{short description|Invariant that plays a role in algebraic geometry and singularity theory}}
In mathematics, and particularly [[singularity theory]], the '''Milnor number''', named after [[John Milnor]], is an invariant of a [[germ (mathematics)|function germ]].

If ''f'' is a complex-valued holomorphic function germ then the Milnor number of ''f'', denoted ''μ''(''f''), is either a nonnegative [[integer]], or is [[Infinity|infinite]]. It can be considered both a [[differential geometry|geometric]] [[Invariant (mathematics)|invariant]] and an [[abstract algebra|algebraic]] invariant. This is why it plays an important role in [[algebraic geometry]] and [[singularity theory]].

== Algebraic definition ==
Consider a holomorphic [[complex numbers|complex]] [[germ (mathematics)|function germ]] 
:<math> f : (\mathbb{C}^n,0) \to (\mathbb{C},0) \  </math> 
and denote by <math>\mathcal{O}_n</math> the [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] of all function germs <math>(\mathbb{C}^n,0) \to (\mathbb{C},0)</math>. 
Every level of a function is a complex hypersurface in <math>\mathbb{C}^n</math>, therefore <math>f</math> is dubbed a hypersurface [[Singular point of an algebraic variety|singularity]].

Assume it is an [[isolated singularity]]: in the case of holomorphic mappings it is said that a hypersurface singularity <math>f</math> is singular at <math>0 \in \mathbb{C}^n</math> if its [[gradient]] <math>\nabla f</math> is zero at <math>0 </math>, and it is said that <math>0 </math> is an isolated singular point if it is the only singular point in a sufficiently small [[neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighbourhood]] of <math>0 </math>. In particular, the multiplicity of the gradient
:<math> \mu(f) = \dim_{\mathbb{C}} \mathcal{O}_n/\nabla f </math>
is finite by an application of [[Hilbert's_Nullstellensatz#Analytic_Nullstellensatz_(Rückert’s_Nullstellensatz)|Rückert's Nullstellensatz]]. This number <math> \mu(f)</math> is the Milnor number of singularity <math> f</math> at <math>0</math>.

Note that the multiplicity of the gradient is finite if and only if the origin is an [[isolated singularity|isolated]] critical point of ''f''.  {{Citation needed|date=August 2025}}

== Geometric interpretation ==
Milnor originally<ref>{{cite book | last=Milnor | first=John | authorlink=John Milnor | title=Singular points of Complex Hypersurfaces | series=Annals of Mathematics Studies | year=1969 | publisher=[[Princeton University Press]]}}</ref> introduced <math>\mu(f)</math> in geometric terms in the following way. All fibers <math> f^{-1}(c) </math> for values <math>c</math> close to <math>0</math> are nonsingular manifolds of real dimension <math>2(n-1)</math>. Their intersection with a small open disc <math>D_{\epsilon}</math> centered at <math>0</math> is a smooth manifold <math>F</math> called the Milnor fiber. Up to diffeomorphism <math>F</math> does not depend on <math>c</math> or <math>\epsilon</math> if they are small enough. It is also diffeomorphic to the fiber of the [[Milnor map|Milnor fibration map]].

The Milnor fiber <math>F</math> is a smooth manifold of dimension <math>2(n-1)</math> and has the same [[Homotopy| homotopy type]] as a [[Wedge sum|bouquet]] of <math>\mu(f)</math> spheres <math>S^{n-1}</math>. This is to say that its middle [[Betti number]]  <math>b_{n-1}(F)</math> is equal to the Milnor number and it has [[Homology (mathematics)|homology]] of a point in dimension less than <math>n-1</math>. For example, a complex [[plane curve]] near every singular point <math>z_0</math> has its Milnor fiber homotopic to [[Rose (topology)|a wedge of <math>\mu_{z_0}(f)</math> circles]] (Milnor number is a local property, so it can have different values at different singular points).

Thus the following equalities hold:
:Milnor number   = number of spheres in the [[Wedge sum|wedge]] = middle [[Betti number]] of <math>F</math> = [[Degree of a continuous mapping|degree of the map]] <math>z\to \frac{{\nabla} f(z)}{\|{\nabla} f(z)\|}</math> on  <math>S_\epsilon</math> = multiplicity of the gradient <math>\nabla f</math>

Another way of looking at Milnor number is by [[Perturbation theory|perturbation]]. It is said that a point is a degenerate singular point, or that ''f'' has a degenerate singularity, at <math>z_0 \in \mathbb{C}^n</math> if <math>z_0</math> is a singular point and the [[Hessian matrix]] of all second order partial derivatives has zero [[determinant]] at <math>z_0</math>:
:<math>  \det\left( \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z_i \partial z_j} \right)_{1 \le i \le j \le n}^{z = z_0} =0. </math>

It is assumed that ''f'' has a degenerate singularity at 0. The multiplicity of this degenerate singularity may be considered by thinking about how many points are [[infinitesimally]] glued. If the image of ''f'' is now [[Perturbation theory|perturbed]] in a certain stable way the isolated degenerate singularity at 0 will split up into other isolated singularities which are non-degenerate. The number of such isolated non-degenerate singularities will be the number of points that have been infinitesimally glued.

Precisely, another function germ ''g'' which is non-singular at the origin is taken and considered the new function germ ''h := f + εg'' where ''ε'' is very small. When ''ε'' = 0 then ''h = f''. The function ''h'' is called the [[Morse theory#Formal development|morsification]] of ''f''. It is very difficult to compute the singularities of ''h'', and indeed it may be computationally impossible. This  number of points that have been [[infinitesimally]] glued, this local multiplicity of ''f'', is exactly the Milnor number of ''f''.

Further contributions<ref>{{Cite book | authorlink1=Vladimir Arnold | last1=Arnold | first1=V.I. | last2=Gusein-Zade | first2=S.M. | last3=Varchenko | first3=A.N. |authorlink3=Alexander Varchenko| title=Singularities of differentiable maps | volume=2 | year=1988 | publisher=[[Birkhäuser]]}}</ref> give meaning to Milnor number in terms of dimension of the space of [[Deformation theory|versal deformations]], i.e. the Milnor number is the minimal dimension of parameter space of deformations that carry all information about initial singularity.

== Examples ==
Given below are some worked examples of polynomials in two variables. Working with only a single variable is too simple and does not give an appropriate illustration of the techniques, whereas working with three variables can be cumbersome. Note that if ''f'' is only [[Holomorphic function|holomorphic]] and not a polynomial, then the [[power series]] expansion of ''f'' can be used.

=== 1 ===

Consider a function germ with a non-degenerate singularity at 0, say <math>f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2</math>. The Jacobian ideal is just <math> \langle 2x, 2y \rangle = \langle x, y \rangle </math>. Computing the local algebra:
:<math> \mathcal{A}_f = \mathcal{O} / \langle x, y \rangle = \langle 1 \rangle . </math>
[[Hadamard's lemma]], which says that any function <math>h\in\mathcal{O}</math> may be written as
:<math> h(x,y) = k + xh_1(x,y) + yh_2(x,y) </math>
for some constant ''k'' and functions <math>h_1</math> and <math>h_2</math> in <math>\mathcal{O}</math> (where either <math>h_1</math> or <math>h_2</math> or both may be exactly zero), justifies this. So, modulo functional multiples of ''x'' and ''y'', the function ''h'' may be written as a constant. The space of constant functions is spanned by 1, hence  <math>\mathcal{A}_f = \langle 1 \rangle</math>

It follows that ''μ''(''f'') = 1. It is easy to check that for any function germ ''g'' with a non-degenerate singularity at 0, ''μ''(''g'') = 1.

Note that applying this method to a non-singular function germ ''g'' yields ''μ''(''g'') = 0.

=== 2 ===

Let <math>f(x,y) = x^3 + xy^2</math>, then
:<math> \mathcal{A}_f = \mathcal{O} / \langle 3x^2 + y^2, xy \rangle = \langle 1, x, y, x^2 \rangle . </math>
So in this case <math>\mu(f) = 4</math>.

=== 3 ===

It may be shown that if <math>f(x,y) = x^2y^2 + y^3</math> then <math>\mu(f) = \infty.</math>

This can be ''explained'' by the fact that ''f'' is singular at every point of the ''x''-axis.

== Versal deformations ==
Let ''f'' have finite Milnor number ''μ'', and let <math>g_1,\ldots, g_{\mu}</math> be a [[Basis (linear algebra)|basis]] for the local algebra, considered as a vector space. Then a miniversal deformation of ''f'' is given by
:<math> F : (\mathbb{C}^n \times \mathbb{C}^{\mu},0) \to (\mathbb{C},0) ,</math>
:<math> F(z,a) := f(z) + a_1g_1(z) + \cdots + a_{\mu}g_{\mu}(z) ,</math>
where <math>(a_1,\dots,a_{\mu})\in \mathbb{C}^{\mu}</math>.
These deformations (or [[unfolding (functions)|unfolding]]s) are of great interest in much of science. {{Citation needed|date=July 2015}}

==Invariance==
Function germs can be collected together to construct [[equivalence class]]es. One standard equivalence is [[A-equivalence|''A''-equivalence]]. It is said that two function germs <math>f,g : (\mathbb{C}^n,0) \to (\mathbb{C},0)</math> are ''A''-equivalent if there exist [[diffeomorphism]] germs <math> \phi : (\mathbb{C}^n,0) \to (\mathbb{C}^n,0)</math> and <math>\psi : (\mathbb{C},0) \to (\mathbb{C},0)</math> such that <math>f \circ \phi = \psi \circ g</math>: there exists a diffeomorphic change of variable in both [[domain of a function|domain]] and [[range of a function|range]] which takes ''f'' to ''g''. If ''f'' and ''g'' are ''A''-equivalent then ''μ''(''f'') = ''μ''(''g'').{{Citation needed|date=July 2024}}

Nevertheless, the Milnor number does not offer a complete invariant for function germs, i.e. the converse is false: there exist function germs ''f'' and ''g'' with ''μ''(''f'') = ''μ''(''g'') which are not ''A''-equivalent. To see this consider <math>f(x,y) = x^3+y^3</math> and <math>g(x,y) = x^2+y^5</math>. This yields <math>\mu(f) = \mu(g) = 4</math> but ''f'' and ''g'' are clearly not ''A''-equivalent since the [[Hessian matrix]] of ''f'' is equal to zero while that of ''g'' is not (and the rank of the Hessian is an ''A''-invariant, as is easy to see).
